summary: Gave mypintusan an ADMINISTRATIVE TRAIL: an append-only record of who changed the rules about who gets in. Item 7 and the last item of the mypintusan hardening register, and the only one on it that was a FEATURE GAP rather than a defect - there was nothing to bench until the trail existed, so the feature and its 66-check live bench landed together. THE GAP. This app keeps the best log in the suite: entities.AccessEvent records every badge presented at every door - who, where, when, granted or denied, and why. What it never recorded is WHO DECIDED THEY COULD. A grant created at 23:40, a holiday deleted the morning of a shutdown, a perimeter door's offline policy flipped from deny to cached, a badge quietly issued to a holder nobody added to the roster: every one of those changes what the access log will say tomorrow, and none of them left a mark that survives. The gap was sharper here than the identical gap was in mymatasan BECAUSE THE ACCESS LOG HIDES IT - a grant edit does not look like an incident, it looks like ordinary green badge rows three weeks later, on a door the person was never meant to reach, with `decision: granted, reason: ok` beside them. The log answers 'did this happen' perfectly and 'was this supposed to happen' not at all. Built on domain/shared/audit, the same append-only table myidsan, myseliasan and mymatasan already use, so bcrypt-grade discipline about field caps, hostile input and retention is one implementation rather than five: new services/audit.go (the action vocabulary and target types), apis/audit.go (GET /api/audit + GET /api/audit.csv, the request-scoped Auditor, and the middleware below), services/metrics.go, app/audit_retention.go. Instrumented: grant create/delete, group create/delete, group membership add/remove, schedule create/delete, holiday create/delete, holder create, credential issue/revoke, door create, remote unlock, lockdown set (BOTH directions - a site sealed during an incident and quietly reopened twenty minutes later is the sequence nobody can reconstruct, because lifting a lockdown produces no event at all, it just makes the denials stop), settings save/reset, and user create/update/delete/password-reset. THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERS, and the reason this is not just a list of Record() calls: the default is RECORDED. apis.NewAuditMiddleware records any ACCEPTED mutating request that reached no handler which audited itself, as `api.write`. A trail instrumented handler-by-handler has this app's own recurring failure mode built into it - seven benches found the same shape seven times, THE MECHANISM IS RIGHT AND NOTHING REACHES IT - and here the symptom would be an empty result in an investigation years later, by which time nobody can tell an appliance where nothing happened from one where the recording was never wired. So a handler's own entry is an ENRICHMENT rather than the only chance, and a route added next year is in the trail on the day it ships. Proven live: POST /api/setup/complete is served by shared code this app does not own, no handler here audits it, and it is in the trail. THE ENTRIES ARE SENTENCES, NOT IDS. A schedule entry carries the HOURS ('Mon 22:00-06:00') because 'schedule created' tells an auditor nothing while the window is what shows somebody widened the night shift to cover 02:00; a grant entry names the group, the door AND the schedule in one line; door.create records the offline policy, the cache TTL and the Secure Channel requirement, because there is no PUT /api/doors and those three values decide what the door does on the day the network is gone; a settings save DIFFS the live values against the save and names only what moved (the screen posts the whole object every time, so the request body cannot answer 'what changed'); a revocation carries the REASON, which is what turns a card presented on Saturday from a denial into an incident. NO SECRET EVER: a rekey is recorded as the fact that a key was replaced, never the key - the trail is readable by every administrator and exported to CSV, and a site base key in it is the exact secret Secure Channel exists to protect. The bench asserts that over EVERY row, plus the absence of passwords and bcrypt hashes. Authorization: /api/audit is admin-only, and /api/audit.csv IS ITS OWN CATALOG RULE - paths match segment-wise, so 'audit.csv' is not governed by 'audit', and a rule covering the listing but not the export would leave the whole trail downloadable by a rule nobody wrote (#224's shape exactly). New viewAudit capability drives a new Admin trail section in the rail, hidden for operator and viewer by the same matrix that refuses the request. New Trail.js screen with filter chips, a CSV export link and localisation in all four languages. New tests: apis/audit_test.go (the middleware's guarantee, no double-recording, reads ignored, the settings diff, and that the trail offers NO write route) and apis/audit_actions_test.go, which reads the source and fails the build if a declared action constant loses its call site - the grep that already found five dead audit constants on myidsan and three unreachable alarms on this app, turned into a build failure, because an absent record and a record of absence look identical in a query. WHAT THE BENCH FOUND: the CSV needed a UTF-8 BOM or Excel on Windows renders every em dash in an auditor's copy as mojibake; and OPENING THE ARABIC PNG showed `card issued to "Screen Bench Person"` rendering as `"card issued to "Screen Bench Person` - the RTL paragraph direction reordering the quotes of a sentence that is deliberately NOT translated (an audit record says what it said; re-rendering it in the reader's language would make the trail's text depend on who is looking), fixed with <bdi dir="ltr">. Every check passed while that was on screen. STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: the middleware runs INSIDE the permission middleware, so a matrix-level 403 is not in the trail (it is in api_log); the branch that records a denial is a handler's own 'administrators only' gate, and in this app's current catalog no role can reach such a route, so that branch is covered by unit test and not on the wire - the bench asserts the true statement instead of a green that means nothing. 66/66 live checks (tools/fleetbench/bench_pintusan_trail.py) and 166/166 on the screen bench with the new section in it.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no breaking API change and no config change required. NEW TABLE: `audit_log`, added additively by the auto-migrator on the next boot - the same shared entity myidsan, myseliasan and mymatasan already carry, so the schema is not new to the suite. Existing installs start recording from that boot; the trail is empty before it, and nothing back-fills, because a record of what happened before there was a recorder would be a fabrication. NEW ENDPOINTS: GET /api/audit and GET /api/audit.csv, both admin-only. There is deliberately NO delete route and NO update route, not even for a superadmin - the value of the trail is that the person whose actions it records cannot edit it. Age-based retention is OFF by default and reachable only from config.json's existing shared `audit` block (enabled/maxRetentionDays/frequencyHours/archiveDir); when switched on it archives to disk and flushes before deleting anything, takes an AGE rather than a selection of rows, and records its own run inside the trail it trimmed. PERMISSIONS: two new catalog rows, both denying viewer and operator, so nothing any role could previously do becomes denied - EnsureApplianceRoles backfills only paths a role has no row for and never edits an existing row's verbs. NEW METRICS: mypintusan_audit_write_failures_total and mypintusan_audit_retention_purged_total; the first exists because the audit service swallows its own write errors on purpose (auditing must never fail the action being audited, and here that action may be somebody standing at a door), which means a trail that has stopped recording otherwise has no symptom at all. The access-rule NOTIFICATIONS are unchanged and are kept alongside the trail: the notification is how a change is noticed now, the trail is how it is proven later. Handler constructor signatures in apps/mypintusan/apis gained an *Auditor parameter; all call sites are in app/app.go and no other app is affected. Frontend adds one nav section and 44 dictionary keys in en/ms/zh/ar. Scope is `infra` rather than `mypintusan`: mypintusan has no entry in infra/versioning/version.json's apps map yet, and an unknown scope token hard-fails the release run.
